units.text: L(2, 1)-labeling of some zero-divisor graphs associated with commutative rings
Introduction
Given a simple undirected finite graph G, and two positive integers j, k, an L(j, k)-labeling of G is a function
f : V (G) −→ Z ≥0 such that |f (v 1 ) − f (v 2 )| ≥ j whenever v 1 is adjacent to v 2 and |f (v 1 ) − f (v 2 )| ≥ k

whenever v 1 and v 2 are at distance two apart.The difference between the maximum and minimum values of f is called span of f , denoted by span(f ).If f is an L(j, k)-labeling of G with minimum value say δ, then the function g defined on vertices of G by g(v) = f (v) − δ is also an L(j, k)-labeling with minimum value 0 and the maximum value as span(f ) = span(g).As a result, we assume that every L(j, k)-labeling has 0 as its minimum value and its span as the maximum value.The minimum span over all L(j, k)-labelings of G is called the L(j, k)-labeling number, denoted by, λ j,k (G).An L(j, k)-labeling f of G is said to be minimal labeling if span(f ) = λ j,k (G).The L(j, k)-labeling problem has been studied extensively for the case j = 2 and k = 1.The L(2, 1)-labeling number of a graph G is called its λ-number, denoted by λ(G).

The difficulty of assigning channel frequencies to transmitters without interference motivates the study of L(j, k)-labeling problem of a graph.Roberts [21] proposed the challenge of efficiently assigning radio channels to transmitters at several sites using non-negative integers to denote channels so that adjacent locations receive distinct channels, and extremely close locations receive channels that are at least at differ by two.As a result, there would be no interference between these channels.In 1992, Griggs and Yeh [9] formalised the concept of L(j, k)-labeling and demonstrated that the L(2, 1)-labeling problem is NPcomplete for general graphs.The L(j, k)-labeling problem and L(2, 1)-labeling problem have been studied in [7,8,12,22].

On the other hand, the fundamental objective of associating a graph to an algebraic structure is to investigate the relationship between algebraic properties and combinatorial properties of algebraic structures.The graphs such as Cayley graph [5], power graph [11], zero-divisor graph [2], group-annhilator [14] and torsion graph [23], are some graphs emerging from algebraic structures such as groups, rings and modules.Beck [3] introduced the concept of an undirected zero-divisor graph Γ ′ (R) which is called Beck's zero-divisor graph of a commutative ring R. In his investigation, all elements of a ring R are vertices of the graph Γ ′ (R) with two distinct vertices u and v adjacent in Γ ′ (R) if and only if uv = 0. Anderson and Livingston [2] also studied the combinatorial properties of a commutative ring R.They associated a graph Γ(R), called the zero-divisor graph, to R with vertices as elements of Z * (R) = Z(R) \ {0}, that is, the non-trivial zero-divisors of R with two vertices u, v ∈ Z * (R) being adjacent in Γ(R) if and only if uv = 0.For more on zero-divisor graphs, please see [1,4,15,16,18,19,20].For basic definitions from graph theory we refer [17].
Let R be a finite commutative ring with unity.A ring R is said to be a local ring if it has a unique maximal ideal.
Let R = R 1 × • • • × R r × F 1 × • • • × F s ,

be the Artinian decomposition of R, where each R i is a commutative local ring with unity, and each F j is a field.A ring R is said to be a mixed ring if either r ≥ 1 and s ≥ 1 or r ≥ 2 and s = 0 in its Artinian decomposition.A ring R is said to be a reduced ring if r = 0 and s ≥ 1 in its Artinian decomposition.This research article is organised as follows.In Section 2, we present some preliminary results and definitions related to L(2, 1)-labeling of graphs.In Section 3, we study partite truncation operation in graphs, and obtain exact value of the λ-number of zero-divisor graphs realized by some classes of reduced rings.
Preliminaries
In this section, we discuss some results related to L(2, 1)-labeling of some classes of graphs.
For a positive real number d, an L d (2, 1)-labeling of a simple graph G is a positive real valued function

f defined on V (G) such that for u 1 , u 2 ∈ V (G), |f (u 1 ) − f (u 2 )| ≥ 2d whenever u 1 is adjacent to u 2 and |f (u 1 ) − f (u 2 )| ≥ d whenever distance between u 1 and u 2 is two. The L d (2, 1)-labeling number of G, denoted by λ(G, d), is the smallest number m such that G has an L d (2, 1)-labeling f with max v∈V (G) {f (v)} = m.

L d (2, 1)-labeling introduced by Griggs and Yeh [9] is a natural generalisation of L(2, 1)-labeling.Note that λ(G, 1) = λ(G).The authors confirmed that to determine λ(G, d), it suffices to study the case for λ(G).They provided bounds on λ-number for a variety of graphs, including trees, cycles, 3-connected graphs and hypercubes.They proved following interesting results in which they obtain upper bounds of λ(G) in terms of graph invariants such as chromatic number χ(G) and maximum degree ∆(G).
Theorem 1 ([9], Theorem 4.1). If G is a graph with n vertices, then λ(G) ≤ n + χ(G) − 2.
Theorem 2 ([9], Theorem 6.2).For any graph G, λ(G) ≤ ∆ 2 (G) + 2∆(G).
The authors in [8] introduced the notion of holes, multiplicities and gaps of an L(2, 1)-labeling.Let f be an L(2, 1)-labeling of G, and given a positive integer h, 0 < h < span(f ), let

f h = {v ∈ V (G) : f (v) = h}. If f h is empty, then h is called a hole of f and if |f h | ≥ 2, then h is called multiplicity of f . h is called a gap of f if h is a hole with |f h−1 | = |f h+1 | = 1 and {v h−1 , v h+1 } ∈ E(G), where f (v h−1 ) = h − 1 and f (v h+1 ) = h + 1. H(f ), M (f )

and G(f ) represents collection of holes, multiplicities and gaps of f respectively.Let h(f ) and g(f ) denote cardinalities of H(f ) and G(f ).The function f is called the minimum L(2, 1)-labeling of G if it is minimal and has minimum number of holes over the set L (2,1) (G), where L (2,1) (G) denotes the set of all minimal L(2, 1)-labelings of G.It should be noted that a minimal L(2, 1)-labeling of a graph G is not unique whereas the minimum L(2, 1)-labeling of a graph G is always unique.For example, if P 6 is a path on six vertices, then the labeling (4, 0, 3, 1, 5, 2) with span as 5 is an L(2, 1)-labeling but not the minimum one, since it is not a minimal L(2, 1)-labeling for P 6 .

The graph invariant called as path covering number is the least number of vertex-disjoint paths required to cover vertices of the graph.The relationship between λ(G) and path covering number c(G) of a graph G proved in [8] is given as follows.

Lemma 3 ([8], Lemma 2.2). Let f be a minimum L(2, 1)-labeling of G. If h is a hole of f , then |f h−1 | = |f h+1 | > 0. Furthermore, if |f h−1 | = |f h+1 | = 1, then h is a gap. Lemma 4 ([8], Lemma 2.3). If f is a minimum L(2, 1)-labeling of G, then G(f ) is empty or M (f ) is empty. Theorem 5 ([8], Theorem 1.1).
Let G be a simple graph of order n, and let G c be its complement.Then the following hold,
(i) λ(G) ≤ n − 1 if and only if c(G c ) = 1. (ii) Let r ≥ 2 be an integer. Then λ(G) = n + r − 2 if and only if c(G c ) = r.

A clique of a graph G is a subset of V (G) such that any two distinct vertices of this subset are adjacent in G.The maximum cardinality of a clique in G is known as its clique number, denoted by ω(G).An independent set of a graph G is a subset of V (G) such that no two vertices in the subset are adjacent.The maximum cardinality of an independent subset in G is called its independence number, denoted by α(G).In [13], the authors investigated the relationships between λ-number and clique number, and also between λ-number and independence number of G.They obtained some interesting results which are presented below.

A p-group is a group in which order of every element is a power of p, where p is a prime number.A finite group is a p-group if and only if its order is a power of a prime p.The Power Graph Γ G [6,11] of a finite group G is the simple graph with vertex set G in which two vertices are adjacent if and only if one is the power of the other.The exact value of λ-number of power graphs of dihedral group D 2n , p-group, and generalised quaternion group Q 4n was computed in [13].For some certain classes of groups of order n, they obtained an upper bound related to λ-number of a power graph.Theorem 8 ([13], Theorem 4.1).If G is a group of order n, where n is not a prime power, then λ(Γ G ) ≤ 2n − 4. The bound is achieved if and only if G is isomorphic to Z 2 × Z 2 or Z 2q , where q is a prime greater than 2.

Furthermore, the L(j, k)-labeling of Cayley graphs has been studied in [24], and Kelarev, Ras, and Zhou [10] revealed a relationship between a semigroup structure and the minimum distance labeling spans of its Cayley graph.
Partite truncation of a graph

In this section, we study a graph operation called as partite truncation of a graph.This operation allows us to obtain a graph of relatively smaller order from a graph of significantly larger order.We prove an interesting result in which we determine the λ-number and a corresponding minimum labeling of Beck's zero-divisor graph Γ ′ (R) from the graph Γ(R) of a ring R, provided that diam(Γ(R)) < 3.

Definition 9. Let G be an n-partite graph with V 1 , V 2 , . . ., V n as partite sets.We define partite truncated graph Ĝ of G with vertices v1 , v2 , . . ., vn , where vi corresponds to the whole partite set V i , 1 ≤ i ≤ n, and two distinct vertices vi and vj are adjacent in Ĝ if and only if there is a vertex in V i adjacent to some vertex in V j .

Thus, in a partite truncation of an n-partite graph, each partite set is truncated to one vertex, and edges (if any) connecting two partite sets are truncated to a single edge.It is clear from the definition that if G is connected, so is Ĝ, and if there is a path between two partite sets V i and V j of G, then there must be a path between the two corresponding vertices vi and vj in Ĝ.If diam(G) = 1, then G ∼ = K n ∼ = Ĝ.Also, if the cardinality of each partite set of G is equal to one, then G ∼ = Ĝ.We consider n-partite graphs G with diam(G) > 1 in which there is at least one partite set V in G of cardinality greater than one.

Let H denote the n-partite graph with the property that the bipartite subgraph induced by any two distinct partite sets V and W is either complete bipartite or empty.If diam(H) = 2, then there are some u, w ∈ V (H) such that d(u, w) = diam(H).If u, w are in two distinct partite sets V, W of H, then d(v, ŵ) = diam( Ĥ) = 2.However, if there are no such vertices u, w lying in two distinct partite sets V, W of H, then diam( Ĥ) = 1.Consequently, diam( Ĥ) ≤ 2 = diam(H).If diam(H) ≥ 3, then it is easy to verify that diam(H) = diam( Ĥ).

In the following result, we see that there is a shift in the λ-number of a graph with a diameter less than three, when a particular number of isolated vertices (set of independent vertices ), and then a dominant vertex (a vertex adjacent to all these isolated vertices and to all other vertices of the graph) are added to it.This subsequently aids in determining the λ-number of Beck's zero-divisor graph Γ ′ (R) of a ring R.

Proof.Let u 1 , u 2 , . . ., u m denote the isolated vertices, and u 0 be the dominant vertex.Also, let f be the minimum labeling of G with holes h 1 , h 2 , . . ., h s .We define L(2, 1)-labeling g on G m+1 as, g(u
0 ) = 0, g(v) = f (v) + 2, for all v ∈ V (G) and g(u i ) = h i + 2, for all i, 1 ≤ i ≤ s. For m > s, g(u s+j ) = λ(G) + j + 2, for all j, 1 ≤ j ≤ m − s.
Therefore,
span(g) = λ(G) + m − s + 2, m > s, λ(G) + 2, m ≤ s.

Since diam(G) < 3, therefore f must be one-to-one.This implies, g is well defined L(2, 1)-labeling of G m+1 .Thus, λ(G m+1 ) ≤ span(g).If we assume that there exist another L(2, 1)-labeling h of G m+1 with span(h) < span(g), then the restriction h ↾ V (G) is a well defined L(2, 1)-labeling of G with span(h ↾ V (G) ) < span(f ), a contradiction.

Next, we provide some examples in which we compute the λ−number of a complete n-partite graph, and λ-number of the zero-divisor graph of a ring F p × F q , where F p and F q are finite fields of order p and q respectively.Example 14.Let K m1,m2,...,mn be a complete n-partite graph, and let V i with |V i | = m i , 1 ≤ i ≤ n, be its partite sets.We assume that there exists at least one m i such that m i > 1.This implies, diam(K m1,m2,...,mn ) = 2. Note, that the partite truncation of K m1,m2,...,mn is isomorphic to K n , and a bipartite subgraph induced by any two distinct partite sets V i and V j is a complete bipartite graph.It is easy to verify that λ(K n ) = 2n − 2.
Thus, by Theorem 12, λ(K m1,m2,...,mn ) =
n i=1 m i + n − 2.

Example 15.Let F p and F q be two finite fields of order p and q, respectively.The set of non-trivial zero divisors of F p × F q and hence the vertices of Γ(F p × F q ) are given as V 1 = {(a, 0) : a ∈ F p and a ̸ = 0}, V 2 = {(0, b) : b ∈ F q and b ̸ = 0}.This implies, |V 1 | = p − 1 and |V 2 | = q − 1.There are no two vertices in sets V 1 or V 2 that are adjacent to each other, and each vertex in V 1 is adjacent to every vertex in V 2 .Thus, Γ(F p × F q ) ∼ = K p−1,q−1 , and consequently, λ(G) = p + q − 2.

Conclusion

In this research article, we studied partite truncation, a graph operation that aids to obtain a smaller order graph from relatively larger order n-partite graph.This contraction of the order allow us to determine the λ-number and corresponding minimal labeling of the n-partite graph from the contracted graph.We exhibited that the zero-divisor graph associated with a Boolean ring is a partite truncated graph of the zerodivisor graph realized by a reduced ring.We also proved an interesting result that illustrates the deduction of λ-number of Beck's zero-divisor graph Γ ′ (R) from λ-number of the zero-divisor graph Γ(R).We concluded this paper with an open problem for future research work.
